title: Industry and Reform
partB: The 1890 law against combinations in restraint of trade, little used against the trusts in its first decade and later the Square Deal's chief legal weapon.
The 1890 killing of hundreds of Lakota by the Seventh Cavalry in South Dakota, which ended the Ghost Dance movement and armed resistance on the northern Plains.
The device by which citizens propose a law themselves and put it directly to the voters, bypassing the legislature.
The Populist and Bryan demand that silver be coined freely at sixteen to one, to expand the currency, raise prices, and ease the burden of debt.
The National Woman's Party pickets who stood silently at the White House gates from 1917, holding banners that quoted the president's own words about democracy.
The 1887 law that broke reservation land into individual allotments and sold the surplus, dissolving much of the Native land base within two generations.
The name Theodore Roosevelt borrowed for the journalists whose exposés in mass-circulation magazines built public opinion for reform.
The urban organization that traded jobs, services, and favors for votes, and ran the Gilded Age city.
